definition: An ordered list of values stored side by side. Each value sits at a numbered position called its index.
Counting positions from 0, so the first item is at index 0 and the last of n items is at index n − 1.
Each value is at least as large as the one before it. Equal neighbours are allowed, so [2, 4, 4, 7] is nondecreasing.
A statement that stays true at every step of an algorithm. Showing it holds at the start and after each step shows the algorithm is correct.
Here, a variable that holds an index, such as left or right. Moving a pointer means changing which position it refers to.
A run of consecutive items from an array, such as positions 2, 3 and 4. A subarray never skips an item.
Items taken from an array in their original order, possibly skipping some. Every subarray is a subsequence, but not the other way round.
The subarray an algorithm is currently looking at, described by its first and last index.
The running total of the first i items. With prefix sums P, the total of positions a to b is P[b + 1] − P[a].
A collection where the last item added is the first one removed (last in, first out), like a pile of plates.
A collection where the first item added is the first one removed (first in, first out), like a line at a counter.
A set of nodes joined by edges, used to model things such as street corners joined by streets.
One point in a graph, such as a street corner. Also called a vertex.
A connection between two nodes. In these lessons edges are undirected: they can be travelled either way.
Every edge counts the same, so the length of a route is simply its number of edges.
In an unweighted graph, the fewest edges on any route between two nodes.
Text that reads the same forwards and backwards, such as “level”.
A letter or a digit. Spaces and punctuation marks are not alphanumeric.
A way to describe how work grows with the input size n. O(n) grows in step with n; O(n²) grows with its square.
Extra memory an algorithm uses beyond its input and output.
Trying every candidate directly. Usually simple and correct, but slow on large inputs.
A chain of nodes where each node holds a value and a link to the next node. You can only reach a node by following links from the start.
Nodes connected without loops, with one root at the top. Each node has children below it; a binary tree has at most two.
A binary tree where every value in a node's left subtree is smaller than the node, and every value in its right subtree is larger.
A tree-shaped structure that always keeps its smallest (or largest) item on top, so that item can be read at once and removed in O(log n).
Solving a problem by calling the same function on a smaller piece of it, until a piece is small enough to answer directly.
Remembering the answer to each smaller problem the first time it is solved, so it is never solved twice.
A range with a start and an end, such as a meeting from 9 to 11. Two intervals overlap when one starts before the other ends.
A table of cells in rows and columns. A cell's neighbours are usually the cells directly above, below, left and right.
A path that returns to where it started, such as a linked list whose last node links back into the list.
An order of tasks in which every task comes after all the tasks it depends on. It exists only when the dependencies have no cycle.
Always moving in one direction: never decreasing, or never increasing.
A smaller version of the problem, such as the same question for the first i items instead of all of them.
A table that stores values under keys and finds any key in about one step on average, no matter how many keys it holds.
